THIRD-PARTY (NONPARENT) CUSTODY AND VISITATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · stepparent

NONPARENT CUSTODY/VISITATION REQUEST — INFORMATION AND DECLARATION
I, Jordan Lee, am not a legal parent of Casey Lee, a minor born January 1, 2018. My relationship to Casey Lee is: stepparent. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual request for custody or visitation of Casey Lee, to be raised within an existing California proceeding of the kind described in Family Code § 3021 (for example, a dissolution, legal separation, nullity, Domestic Violence Prevention Act, or Uniform Parentage Act proceeding), under the standards described in Family Code §§ 3040, 3041, and 3100. This declaration is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not grant Jordan Lee custody or visitation of Casey Lee. Casey Lee's parent(s) of record, so far as known, are Taylor Morgan and Riley Chen, where applicable. Only a court order issued after the applicable proceeding, notice, and hearing process — including, where a parent objects to custody, the finding of detriment to the child that Family Code § 3041 requires — can grant custody, and only a court's own determination that visitation is in Casey Lee's best interest under the applicable statute can grant visitation.

THE GENERAL CUSTODY PREFERENCE ORDER, INCLUDING A NONPARENT — FAMILY CODE § 3040(A)
California Family Code § 3040(a) states the order of preference a court applies when awarding custody of Casey Lee, according to Casey Lee's best interest: first, "[t]o both parents jointly ... or to either parent"; second, "[i]f to neither parent, to the person or persons in whose home the child has been living in a wholesome and stable environment"; and third, "[t]o any other person or persons deemed by the court to be suitable and able to provide adequate and proper care and guidance for the child." This third-tier language is the statutory hook that allows a nonparent — such as Jordan Lee, if Jordan Lee is not Casey Lee's legal parent — to be awarded custody at all, but only where the first two, parent-preferring tiers do not apply.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Custody should be granted in the following order of preference according to the best interest of the child as provided in Sections 3011 and 3020: (1) To both parents jointly pursuant to Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 3080) or to either parent. In making an order granting custody to either parent, the court shall consider, among other factors, which parent is more likely to allow the child frequent and continuing contact with the noncustodial parent, consistent with Sections 3011 and 3020. The court, in its discretion, may require the parents to submit to the court a plan for the implementation of the custody order. (2) If to neither parent, to the person or persons in whose home the child has been living in a wholesome and stable environment. (3) To any other person or persons deemed by the court to be suitable and able to provide adequate and proper care and guidance for the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3040(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3040(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3040.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's general custody preference order — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that a nonparent's suitability alone entitles that nonparent to custody. This clause cites a single statutory subsection, § 3040(a); no additional independent source was found for it. Section 3040(a) does not itself define "wholesome and stable environment" or "suitable and able to provide adequate and proper care," and this clause does not resolve what either phrase means on any specific family's facts. Separately, and importantly, § 3040(a) states this preference order but does not itself state the heightened finding a court must make before awarding custody to a nonparent over a parent's objection — that heightened finding is addressed in this document's companion clause on Family Code § 3041 — nor does § 3040(a) itself give a nonparent standing to bring a custody request; standing is addressed in this document's companion clause on Family Code § 3021.

THE HEIGHTENED DETRIMENT FINDING REQUIRED TO AWARD A NONPARENT CUSTODY OVER A PARENT'S OBJECTION, AND THE STATUTE'S OWN DEFINITION OF "DETRIMENT" — FAMILY CODE § 3041(A)-(C)
Family Code § 3041(a) states that "[b]efore making an order granting custody to a person other than a parent, over the objection of a parent, the court shall make a finding that granting custody to a parent would be detrimental to the child and that granting custody to the nonparent is required to serve the best interest of the child." The same subdivision states that "[a]llegations that parental custody would be detrimental to the child, other than a statement of that ultimate fact, shall not appear in the pleadings." Under § 3041(b), "a finding that parental custody would be detrimental to the child shall be supported by clear and convincing evidence" — a heightened evidentiary standard, subject to a different, lower standard the same section separately provides for in subdivision (d). Section 3041(c) itself defines the key term: "'detriment to the child' includes the harm of removal from a stable placement of a child with a person who has assumed, on a day-to-day basis, the role of the child's parent, fulfilling both the child's physical needs and the child's psychological needs for care and affection, and who has assumed that role for a substantial period of time," and the same subdivision states that "[a] finding of detriment does not require a finding of unfitness of the parents."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Before making an order granting custody to a person other than a parent, over the objection of a parent, the court shall make a finding that granting custody to a parent would be detrimental to the child and that granting custody to the nonparent is required to serve the best interest of the child. Allegations that parental custody would be detrimental to the child, other than a statement of that ultimate fact, shall not appear in the pleadings."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3041(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3041(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3041.)
  "Subject to subdivision (d), a finding that parental custody would be detrimental to the child shall be supported by clear and convincing evidence."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3041(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3041(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3041.)
  "As used in this section, “detriment to the child” includes the harm of removal from a stable placement of a child with a person who has assumed, on a day-to-day basis, the role of the child’s parent, fulfilling both the child’s physical needs and the child’s psychological needs for care and affection, and who has assumed that role for a substantial period of time. A finding of detriment does not require a finding of unfitness of the parents."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3041(c) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3041(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3041.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the heightened detriment finding governing nonparent custody over a parent's objection, and of that statute's own definition of "detriment to the child" — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that meeting this standard alone guarantees any particular custody outcome. This clause cites three subsections of the same statutory section, § 3041(a), (b), and (c); no additional independent source beyond § 3041 itself was found for this. This corrects an assumption in the research request that prompted this clause: "detriment to the child" is not left entirely to case law to define — § 3041(c)'s own text gives it express statutory content, centered on removal from a person who has assumed a day-to-day parental role for a substantial period of time — although the statute's use of the word "includes" signals that this definition is illustrative rather than necessarily exhaustive, and how it applies to any specific family's facts is not resolved by the statute's text alone. This clause does not address § 3041(d), which creates a separate, lower preponderance-of-the-evidence presumption for a person who meets the § 3041(c) description, or § 3041(e), which applies distinct evidentiary standards under the Indian Child Welfare Act; neither subdivision (d) nor (e) was independently verified for inclusion as a quoted citation in this document.

THE GENERAL, DISCRETIONARY NONPARENT VISITATION PROVISION — FAMILY CODE § 3100(A)
Family Code § 3100(a) is the statutory chapeau of California's Chapter 5 visitation-rights framework. After stating the standard for visitation between Casey Lee and a parent, the same subdivision provides, in a single additional sentence: "In the discretion of the court, reasonable visitation rights may be granted to any other person having an interest in the welfare of the child." This is the general, catch-all statutory basis for a nonparent — someone other than Casey Lee's legal parent, and other than a grandparent (whose visitation rights arise under the separate statutes addressed in this corpus's Grandparent Visitation document) — to be granted visitation with Casey Lee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In the discretion of the court, reasonable visitation rights may be granted to any other person having an interest in the welfare of the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3100(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3100(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3100.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the general, discretionary nonparent visitation provision within California's visitation-rights chapter — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that having "an interest in the welfare of the child" by itself entitles any particular person to visitation. This clause cites a single statutory subsection, § 3100(a); no additional independent source was found for it. This corrects a framing assumption in the research request that prompted this clause: Family Code § 3101 is not the general nonparent visitation provision — its own text, addressed in this document's companion clause, is limited specifically to stepparents. The broader, catch-all "any other person having an interest in the welfare of the child" language instead appears in § 3100(a) itself. Section 3100(a)'s grant of discretion is also textually tied to "making an order pursuant to Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 3080)" — meaning it operates within an existing custody-related order-making process, not as its own freestanding petition mechanism; this document's companion clause on Family Code § 3021 addresses that procedural threshold separately. This clause does not restate § 3100(b) through (f), which address visitation limits and safeguards in cases involving a protective order, domestic violence, or a confidential shelter address, and which were not independently verified for inclusion as quoted citations in this document.

STEPPARENT VISITATION IS A SEPARATE, NARROWER STATUTORY PATHWAY — FAMILY CODE § 3101(A), (C)
Alongside the general, discretionary nonparent visitation provision in Family Code § 3100(a), California provides a separate, more specific pathway for a stepparent. Family Code § 3101(a) provides: "Notwithstanding any other provision of law, the court may grant reasonable visitation to a stepparent, if visitation by the stepparent is determined to be in the best interest of the minor child." That grant has an express limit: § 3101(c) states that "[v]isitation rights may not be ordered under this section that would conflict with a right of custody or visitation of a birth parent who is not a party to the proceeding." Section 3101(d)(2) defines "stepparent," for purposes of this section, as "a person who is a party to the marriage that is the subject of the proceeding, with respect to a minor child of the other party to the marriage" — a narrower category than "any other person having an interest in the welfare of the child" under § 3100(a).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Notwithstanding any other provision of law, the court may grant reasonable visitation to a stepparent, if visitation by the stepparent is determined to be in the best interest of the minor child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3101(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3101(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3101.)
  "Visitation rights may not be ordered under this section that would conflict with a right of custody or visitation of a birth parent who is not a party to the proceeding."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3101(c) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3101(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3101.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a distinct, stepparent-specific visitation pathway — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that this document exhaustively covers stepparent visitation or stepparent adoption (a separate document elsewhere in this corpus addresses stepparent adoption specifically, which is a different legal mechanism entirely). This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 3101(a) and (c); the definitional subdivision § 3101(d)(2) is paraphrased rather than separately quoted as its own citation. Because § 3101's own definition of "stepparent" is tied to being "a party to the marriage that is the subject of the proceeding," it does not, by its terms, extend to a former stepparent whose marriage to the child's parent has ended, to an unmarried partner of a parent, or to a former domestic partner who is not a stepparent as the statute defines that term — such a person's visitation request, if any, would fall instead under the general § 3100(a) provision addressed in this document's companion clause, not under this section. This clause does not resolve whether any specific person qualifies as a "stepparent" under § 3101(d)(2) on particular facts.

NONPARENT CUSTODY AND VISITATION DETERMINATIONS ARISE WITHIN AN ALREADY-PENDING PROCEEDING, NOT A FREESTANDING PETITION — FAMILY CODE § 3021
Family Code § 3021 defines the scope of Part 2 of Division 8 of the Family Code — the part of the Family Code that contains both the general custody-preference and detriment provisions (§§ 3040, 3041) and the general nonparent visitation provision (§ 3100(a)) addressed in this document's other clauses. Section 3021 provides: "This part applies in any of the following: (a) A proceeding for dissolution of marriage. (b) A proceeding for nullity of marriage. (c) A proceeding for legal separation of the parties. (d) An action for exclusive custody pursuant to Section 3120. (e) A proceeding to determine physical or legal custody or for visitation in a proceeding pursuant to the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200)). ... (f) A proceeding to determine physical or legal custody or visitation in an action pursuant to the Uniform Parentage Act (Part 3 (commencing with Section 7600) of Division 12). (g) A proceeding to determine physical or legal custody or visitation in an action brought by the district attorney pursuant to Section 17404." Unlike the grandparent-specific statute addressed in this corpus's separate Grandparent Visitation document, which lets a grandparent file a freestanding petition under Family Code § 3104 without any other proceeding pending, Part 2's general custody and visitation provisions apply only inside one of the proceeding types § 3021 lists.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "This part applies in any of the following: (a) A proceeding for dissolution of marriage. (b) A proceeding for nullity of marriage. (c) A proceeding for legal separation of the parties. (d) An action for exclusive custody pursuant to Section 3120. (e) A proceeding to determine physical or legal custody or for visitation in a proceeding pursuant to the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200)). ... (f) A proceeding to determine physical or legal custody or visitation in an action pursuant to the Uniform Parentage Act (Part 3 (commencing with Section 7600) of Division 12). (g) A proceeding to determine physical or legal custody or visitation in an action brought by the district attorney pursuant to Section 17404."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3021 (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 3021 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3021.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's general nonparent custody and visitation provisions operate within an already-pending or properly commenced proceeding rather than through their own freestanding petition mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This clause cites a single statutory section, § 3021, and quotes it with one internal sentence (a caveat within subdivision (e) about Domestic Violence Prevention Act proceedings and established parent-child relationships) omitted for length, marked by ellipsis; no additional independent source was found for this. This clause corrects an assumption in the research request that prompted it: the general nonparent custody and visitation provisions in Family Code §§ 3040, 3041, and 3100(a) do not themselves state what gives a nonparent standing to start a case — the statute's own text does not describe a nonparent-initiated freestanding petition comparable to grandparent visitation's § 3104 mechanism. Instead, a nonparent's practical route into one of the § 3021 proceeding types (for example, becoming a party to a pending dissolution, legal separation, Domestic Violence Prevention Act, or Uniform Parentage Act proceeding, or bringing a Uniform Parentage Act action) is a fact- and procedure-specific question this clause does not resolve, and this document does not verify or address the entirely separate Probate Code guardianship process, which is a distinct, non-Family-Code mechanism by which a nonparent can obtain custody-like authority over a child and which was not researched for this document. This clause also notes, without independently quoting it as a separate citation, that § 3021(d)'s cross-referenced exclusive-custody action under Family Code § 3120 is by that section's own text available only to "a spouse" — not to a nonparent — so § 3120 does not itself supply nonparent standing either.

CROSS-REFERENCE: THE CONSTITUTIONAL BACKDROP FOR NONPARENT CUSTODY AND VISITATION ORDERS
The heightened detriment finding Family Code § 3041 requires before a court awards a nonparent custody over a parent's objection, and the discretionary nature of Family Code § 3100(a)'s nonparent visitation provision, operate against a constitutional backdrop the U.S. Supreme Court articulated in Troxel v. Granville (2000) 530 U.S. 57: "In light of this extensive precedent, it cannot now be doubted that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment protects the fundamental right of parents to make decisions concerning the care, custody, and control of their children."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In light of this extensive precedent, it cannot now be doubted that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment protects the fundamental right of parents to make decisions concerning the care, custody, and control of their children."
  — Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) (U.S. Supreme Court, plurality opinion of O'Connor, J.), 530 U.S. 57, 66 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1087668/troxel-v-granville/)
  Known gap: This citation and its exact quoted text are reused from this corpus's existing, already-verified Grandparent Visitation document (clause grandvis_3104b_filing_restriction) rather than independently re-fetched from CourtListener during this session; that reuse is disclosed here rather than presented as a fresh verification. Troxel addressed a Washington visitation statute, Wash. Rev. Code § 26.10.160(3), not any California statute, and its plurality opinion did not construe Family Code § 3040, § 3041, or § 3100 specifically. This session did not locate or verify any California case law applying Troxel's holding directly to §§ 3040, 3041, or 3100(a) the way California's courts have applied it to the grandparent-specific § 3104(e) and (f) presumptions (addressed in this corpus's existing grandvis_3104ef_presumptions clause, citing In re Marriage of Harris (2004) 34 Cal.4th 210) — that case-law connection was not researched for this document and is not claimed here. This clause states Troxel's general constitutional principle as background context for why California's nonparent custody and visitation statutes require the specific findings and presumptions described in this document's other clauses, not as a holding that Troxel itself resolved any question under §§ 3040, 3041, or 3100.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT BLOCK — NONPARENT CUSTODY/VISITATION INFORMATION SHEET
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on October 1, 2026 at San Francisco, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual request for custody or visitation raised within a pending California proceeding of the kind described in Family Code § 3021, in the San Francisco County Superior Court or other court of competent jurisdiction. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that request, and it does not grant custody or visitation rights; only a court order does that.]

Because § 3101's own definition of "stepparent" is tied to being "a party to the marriage that is the subject of the proceeding," it does not, by its terms, extend to a former stepparent whose marriage to the child's parent has ended, to an unmarried partner of a parent, or to a former domestic partner who is not a stepparent as the statute defines that term — such a person's visitation request, if any, would fall instead under the general § 3100(a) provision addressed in this document's companion clause, not under this section. This clause does not resolve whether any specific person qualifies as a "stepparent" under § 3101(d)(2) on particular facts.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code § 3021 defines the scope of Part 2 of Division 8 of the Family Code — the part of the Family Code that contains both the general custody-preference and detriment provisions (§§ 3040, 3041) and the general nonparent visitation provision (§ 3100(a)) addressed in this document's other clauses. Section 3021 provides: "This part applies in any of the following: (a) A proceeding for dissolution of marriage. (b) A proceeding for nullity of marriage. (c) A proceeding for legal separation of the parties. (d) An action for exclusive custody pursuant to Section 3120. (e) A proceeding to determine physical or legal custody or for visitation in a proceeding pursuant to the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200)). ... (f) A proceeding to determine physical or legal custody or visitation in an action pursuant to the Uniform Parentage Act (Part 3 (commencing with Section 7600) of Division 12). (g) A proceeding to determine physical or legal custody or visitation in an action brought by the district attorney pursuant to Section 17404." Unlike the grandparent-specific statute addressed in this corpus's separate Grandparent Visitation document, which lets a grandparent file a freestanding petition under Family Code § 3104 without any other proceeding pending, Part 2's general custody and visitation provisions apply only inside one of the proceeding types § 3021 lists.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's general nonparent custody and visitation provisions operate within an already-pending or properly commenced proceeding rather than through their own freestanding petition mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This clause cites a single statutory section, § 3021, and quotes it with one internal sentence (a caveat within subdivision (e) about Domestic Violence Prevention Act proceedings and established parent-child relationships) omitted for length, marked by ellipsis; no additional independent source was found for this. This clause corrects an assumption in the research request that prompted it: the general nonparent custody and visitation provisions in Family Code §§ 3040, 3041, and 3100(a) do not themselves state what gives a nonparent standing to start a case — the statute's own text does not describe a nonparent-initiated freestanding petition comparable to grandparent visitation's § 3104 mechanism. Instead, a nonparent's practical route into one of the § 3021 proceeding types (for example, becoming a party to a pending dissolution, legal separation, Domestic Violence Prevention Act, or Uniform Parentage Act proceeding, or bringing a Uniform Parentage Act action) is a fact- and procedure-specific question this clause does not resolve, and this document does not verify or address the entirely separate Probate Code guardianship process, which is a distinct, non-Family-Code mechanism by which a nonparent can obtain custody-like authority over a child and which was not researched for this document. This clause also notes, without independently quoting it as a separate citation, that § 3021(d)'s cross-referenced exclusive-custody action under Family Code § 3120 is by that section's own text available only to "a spouse" — not to a nonparent — so § 3120 does not itself supply nonparent standing either.

expectedJSON.body: The heightened detriment finding Family Code § 3041 requires before a court awards a nonparent custody over a parent's objection, and the discretionary nature of Family Code § 3100(a)'s nonparent visitation provision, operate against a constitutional backdrop the U.S. Supreme Court articulated in Troxel v. Granville (2000) 530 U.S. 57: "In light of this extensive precedent, it cannot now be doubted that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment protects the fundamental right of parents to make decisions concerning the care, custody, and control of their children."
